backlog.title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
backlog.summary: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a…

AlphaGo’s success relied on a dual-system architecture that combined intuitive pattern recognition with a search tree to evaluate future consequences, a capability absent in current generative models.
The author contends that achieving trustworthy results in high-stakes fields like medicine requires moving beyond probabilistic text prediction toward explicit, tree-based reasoning architectures.

backlog.title: Row-Parallel DRAM Computing Cuts Data-Reorganization Overhead (Syracuse, FAU, TU Dresden)
backlog.summary:
Researchers at Syracuse University, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, and TU Dresden published a technical paper titled “RAPID: Row-Parallel Arithmetic Processing in DRAM.” Abstract Excerpt: “Processing-using-memory (PUM) architectures perform computation directly within DRAM to reduce costly data movement between memory and processors. Because charge-sharing operations are confined to individual bitlines, existing DRAM-PUM architectures reorganize data into column-oriented, bit-serial... » read more
The post Row-Parallel DRAM Computing Cuts Data-Reorganization Overhead (Syracuse, FAU, TU Dresden) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: The RAPID architecture introduces row-parallel arithmetic processing within DRAM to eliminate the costly data-reorganization overhead typical of existing processing-using-memory (PUM) designs.
By adding migration and inversion cells to DRAM subarrays, the system enables horizontal data movement and logical operations without converting data to bit-serial formats.
This approach preserves CPU-compatible, word-parallel layouts, allowing for more efficient integration of in-memory computing with conventional processor architectures.

Backside power... » read more
The post Backside Clock Meshes Cut Skew and Power in 2nm Nanosheets (UCSC) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers at UCSC have performed the first design-space exploration of backside clock meshes specifically for 2nm GAAFET nanosheet technology.
By utilizing backside power delivery networks, designers can implement thick, low-resistance metal layers to reduce clock skew and power consumption.
The study highlights the architectural challenge of connecting backside meshes to frontside flip-flops, which necessitates the use of through-silicon vias (TSVs).

A monolithically integrated... » read more

bullets: Researchers have demonstrated a monolithically integrated memristor-TFT stack that enables electrically programmable temporal dynamics for reservoir computing.

bullets: Researchers from Infineon and TU Munich argue that abstraction is the defining characteristic of hardware engineering models, enabling complexity management at the cost of inherent incompleteness.

bullets: How complementary inspection and metrology techniques can detect smaller defects and distinguish among a wide range of defect types within a unified workflow.

bullets: More measurements don’t eliminate blind spots when each view captures only part of the device.

Advanced chips now come with an extraordinary amount of evidence about them.

They’re modeled before they exist, measured during fabrication, inspected during assembly, electrically tested at the wafer and package levels, characterized under thermal and power loads, and increasingly monitored...
In some ways, engineers can see more of a device than ever before.
The problem is that each of those views is partial.

Key Takeaways:
Semiconductor fabs are leveraging AI/ML models and raw equipment data to speed up yield learning, but the volume of data they are collecting — in some cases, hundreds of petabytes a year — is forcing...
The amount of data they are wrestling with has exploded due to increased sampling from inspection and metrology tools, which is used to detect yield issues.
This includes data that is streaming from equipment sensors, which is a relatively new contributor to the data volume.

AI/ML inference models use this sensor data for in-situ analysis, which enables more responsive advanced process control (APC) and quicker identification of changes that could adversely impact downstream yield.
